provenance.source: NCERT Mathematics Class 8, Chapter 1 'Rational Numbers'. Definitions and standard form follow the textbook; the misconception list is not from the book — it is the set of errors that show up when Class 8 students are asked these questions, and each one is written so a distractor can point at it.
provenance.note: The mathematics here is self-checking and does not depend on which NCERT printing a school uses. The CHAPTER NUMBER does: NCERT is mid-transition under NCF-SE 2023 and the Class 8 book is being replaced. Confirm 'Rational Numbers' is still chapter 1 in the book your students hold before showing a chapter number in the UI. Prose translated to en-IN by scripts/translate-pack.ts using gpt-5.5 (135 of 135 strings); LaTeX, answers and distractor maps unchanged by construction. Not read by a subject expert since.

concepts.title: What a rational number is
concepts.statement: A rational number is a number that can be written in the form $\frac{p}{q}$, where $p$ and $q$ are both integers and $q \neq 0$. Every integer is also rational, because $5$ can be written as $\frac{5}{1}$.
concepts.hook: Think of a pizza cut into 8 equal pieces, and you ate 3 of them. You ate $\frac{3}{8}$ of the pizza. Now think that you ate the whole pizza — that is $\frac{8}{8}$, meaning 1. And if you did not eat even one piece, that is $\frac{0}{8}$, meaning 0. All three — 3 pieces, the whole, and nothing — are rational numbers. The question is: can a pizza be divided into 0 pieces?

analogies.text: Rupees and paise: 75 paise means $\frac{75}{100}$ rupees. Every paisa is a rational number.
Cricket run rate: 240 runs in 50 overs means $\frac{240}{50}$ = 4.8 runs per over. Run rate is always a rational number.

formulas.note: This is the definition. q ≠ 0 is the most important condition.
That is why every integer is rational.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Only fractions are rational numbers. A whole number like 7 is not rational.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The definition says the number SHOULD BE ABLE to be written in the form $\frac{p}{q}$ — not that it must already look like a fraction. 7 can be written as $\frac{7}{1}$, so 7 is rational.
misconceptions.correction: Every integer is rational. Put denominator 1, and it is done.
misconceptions.probe: Can you write 7 in the form $\frac{p}{q}$? If yes, then is 7 rational?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: $\frac{5}{0}$ means 0, or it means a very large number.
misconceptions.why_wrong: $\frac{5}{0}$ has no meaning at all. Division means 'into how many equal parts it is divided' — dividing into 0 parts is not even a valid action. So q ≠ 0 is part of the definition, not an extra rule.
misconceptions.correction: The denominator is never 0. $\frac{5}{0}$ is not a rational number at all — it is undefined.
misconceptions.probe: Between $\frac{0}{5}$ and $\frac{5}{0}$, which one is a rational number and which one is not a number at all?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Negative numbers are not rational, because we cannot see them as pieces.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The definition says p and q are integers — and integers include negative numbers too. In $-\frac{3}{4}$, p = -3, which is an integer.
misconceptions.correction: $-\frac{3}{4}$ is completely rational. Being negative is not a problem.
misconceptions.probe: In $-\frac{3}{4}$, what is p and what is q? Are both integers?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 0 is not a rational number because it is 'nothing'.
misconceptions.why_wrong: 0 can be written as $\frac{0}{1}$ — p = 0 is an integer, q = 1 is an integer and is not 0. Both conditions are satisfied.
misconceptions.correction: 0 is rational. The numerator can be 0; only the denominator cannot be 0.
misconceptions.probe: What is the value of $\frac{0}{7}$, and is it a rational number?

worked_examples.problem: Say whether $-6$ is a rational number or not. Give a reason.
steps: To be rational, the number must be writable as $\frac{p}{q}$, with p and q as integers, q ≠ 0
Here p = -6 (an integer) and q = 1 (an integer, and not 0)

worked_examples.problem: Which of $\frac{0}{9}$ and $\frac{9}{0}$ is a rational number?
steps: $\frac{0}{9}$: here q = 9, which is not 0. The condition is satisfied — this is rational, and its value is 0
$\frac{9}{0}$: here q = 0. The definition says q ≠ 0
So $\frac{9}{0}$ is not a rational number at all — it is undefined

concepts.title: Standard form of a rational number
concepts.statement: A rational number is in standard form when its denominator is positive and the numerator and denominator have no common factor except 1. For example, the standard form of $\frac{-12}{18}$ is $\frac{-2}{3}$.
concepts.hook: Think that you went to a shop and asked for 500 gram sugar. The shopkeeper said 'half kilo'. Both mean the same thing, but 'half kilo' is easier to say. Standard form is the same — the same number, written in the clearest way. Question: $\frac{-12}{18}$ and $\frac{12}{-18}$ — are these two different numbers?

analogies.text: Writing an address: '3rd floor, flat 12' and 'flat 12, 3rd floor' — it is the same house, but one way is standard and everyone understands it.
Score 6/10 and 3/5 — the same performance, but 3/5 is written with smaller numbers.

formulas.note: Dividing by the HCF gives the standard form.
To make the denominator positive, change the sign of both the numerator and the denominator.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Standard form means only making the denominator positive. Dividing by the HCF is not needed.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Standard form has two conditions, not one: the denominator MUST be positive, and the numerator and denominator MUST be coprime. The denominator of $\frac{-12}{18}$ is already positive, but it is still not in standard form.
misconceptions.correction: Do two things — fix the sign, then divide by the HCF. Without both, it is not standard form.
misconceptions.probe: The denominator of $\frac{-12}{18}$ is positive. Still, why is it not in standard form?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: In standard form, the numerator must always be positive.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The condition is on the denominator, not on the numerator. $\frac{-2}{3}$ is fully in standard form — denominator 3 is positive, and 2 and 3 are coprime.
misconceptions.correction: The denominator must be positive. The numerator can be negative.
misconceptions.probe: Is $\frac{-2}{3}$ in standard form or not? Which condition should we check — numerator or denominator?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: $\frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{4}{6}$ are two different rational numbers.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Both have exactly the same value — in $\frac{4}{6}$, divide the numerator and denominator by 2 and you get $\frac{2}{3}$. Different writing, same number.
misconceptions.correction: Equivalent rational numbers are not different numbers; they are different forms of the same number. On the number line, both sit at the same place.
misconceptions.probe: Divide the numerator and denominator of $\frac{4}{6}$ by 2. What do you get? So is it a different number from $\frac{2}{3}$?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: To find the standard form, divide the numerator and denominator by any common number — it just has to become smaller.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Dividing by any common factor makes the numbers smaller, but it may not give the standard form. Dividing $\frac{12}{18}$ by 2 gives $\frac{6}{9}$ — 6 and 9 still have 3 in common.
misconceptions.correction: Divide by the HCF, not by just any common factor. After the HCF, nothing common is left.
misconceptions.probe: When $\frac{12}{18}$ is divided by 2, we get $\frac{6}{9}$. Is this standard form? Is anything common left in 6 and 9?

steps: Denominator 18 is already positive, so we do not have to do the sign step
Divide both the numerator and the denominator by 6: $\frac{-12 \div 6}{18 \div 6} = \frac{-2}{3}$
Check: 2 and 3 have nothing common except 1. Done
The denominator is negative, so first change the sign of both the numerator and the denominator: $\frac{14}{-35} = \frac{-14}{35}$
Denominator 5 is positive, and 2 and 5 are coprime

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a rational number?
questions.solution: The condition for a rational number is $q \neq 0$. In $\frac{7}{0}$, the denominator is 0, so it is not a rational number at all — it is undefined. The other three are rational: $\frac{0}{7} = 0$, $-7 = \frac{-7}{1}$, and $\frac{-7}{2}$ is already in the form $\frac{p}{q}$.

questions.stem: How will we write $5$ in the form $\frac{p}{q}$?

options.text: $5$ cannot be written in the form $\frac{p}{q}$ at all

questions.solution: $5 = \frac{5}{1}$. Here p = 5 and q = 1, both are integers and q ≠ 0 — so 5 is a rational number.

options.text: It is a rational number and its value is 0
It is not a rational number, because 0 is not rational
It is rational, but its value is 9

questions.solution: In $\frac{0}{9}$, the denominator is 9, which is not 0 — so the condition is satisfied. Its value is $0$. It would be undefined if the denominator were 0, like $\frac{9}{0}$.

questions.stem: Which of these are rational numbers? (More than one can be correct)
questions.solution: $-4 = \frac{-4}{1}$ is rational, $\frac{0}{3} = 0$ is rational, $\frac{-5}{8}$ is rational. Only $\frac{3}{0}$ is not rational because the denominator is 0.

questions.stem: If $\frac{p}{7}$ is a rational number and its value is $-2$, then what will be the value of $p$?
Riya says: 'Every integer is rational, but every rational number is not an integer.' What kind of statement is this?

options.text: It is correct — $5 = \frac{5}{1}$ is both an integer and rational, but $\frac{1}{2}$ is rational and not an integer
It is wrong — no integer is rational
It is wrong — every rational number is an integer
It is correct, but only for positive numbers

questions.solution: Every integer $n$ can be written as $\frac{n}{1}$, so every integer is rational. The reverse is not true: $\frac{1}{2}$ is rational but not an integer. Negative numbers do not change this.

questions.stem: Explain why $\frac{a}{0}$ cannot be a rational number for any $a$, no matter how large $a$ is.

rubric: Rational number ki definition batayi: $\frac{p}{q}$ jahan q ≠ 0
Bhaag ka matlab samjhaya — 0 barabar hisson me baantna ek kaam hi nahi hai
Ya: agar $\frac{a}{0} = x$ hota to $a = x \times 0 = 0$ hona chahiye, jo har a ke liye sach nahi
Nateeja: $\frac{a}{0}$ undefined hai, bada number nahi

questions.solution: Suppose $\frac{a}{0} = x$. By the definition of division, $a = x \times 0 = 0$. This means it can happen only when $a = 0$, and even then $x$ can be any number — there is no single answer. So $\frac{a}{0}$ has no value at all. It is not a 'very large number'; it is undefined.

questions.stem: What is the standard form of $\frac{-12}{18}$?
questions.solution: HCF(12, 18) = 6. Divide both the numerator and the denominator by 6: $\frac{-12 \div 6}{18 \div 6} = \frac{-2}{3}$. Dividing by 2 gives $\frac{-6}{9}$, in which 3 is still common — that is not standard form.

In standard form, the denominator must be positive. Change the sign of both the numerator and the denominator: $\frac{4}{-9} = \frac{-4}{9}$. 4 and 9 have nothing common except 1, so this is the standard form.

questions.stem: Which rational number is NOT equal to $\frac{2}{3}$?
questions.solution: $\frac{4}{6}$, $\frac{-2}{-3}$ and $\frac{10}{15}$ — all three have value $\frac{2}{3}$. The value of $\frac{-4}{6}$ is $\frac{-2}{3}$, which is negative.

questions.stem: Which of these is already in standard form?
questions.solution: $\frac{-5}{7}$: denominator 7 is positive and HCF(5, 7) = 1. Both conditions are satisfied. The denominator of $\frac{5}{-7}$ is negative; $\frac{10}{14}$ and $\frac{-10}{14}$ have 2 in common.

questions.stem: The standard form of $\frac{-45}{60}$ is $\frac{p}{q}$. What will be the value of $p + q$?
Arjun found the standard form of $\frac{24}{-36}$ as $\frac{-4}{6}$. What is his mistake?

options.text: He divided by 6, but the HCF is 12 — 4 and 6 still have 2 in common
There is no mistake, $\frac{-4}{6}$ is the correct answer
He made the sign wrong; the answer should be $\frac{4}{6}$
He reversed it; the answer should be $\frac{-6}{4}$

questions.solution: HCF(24, 36) = 12, not 6. The correct answer is $\frac{24}{-36} = \frac{-24}{36} = \frac{-2}{3}$. Arjun got the sign right — the only mistake was that he did not find the full HCF.

questions.stem: A rational number has infinitely many equivalent forms, but only one standard form. Explain why this is so.

rubric: Equivalent roop banane ka tareeka: upar-neeche dono ko kisi bhi non-zero integer se guna karo
Aise integers anant hain, isliye equivalent roop anant hain
Standard form ki do shartein: denominator positive, aur HCF = 1
In dono shartein ek saath sirf ek hi jodi (p, q) pe poori hoti hain, isliye standard form unique hai

questions.solution: $\frac{2}{3}$ can be written as $\frac{4}{6}, \frac{6}{9}, \frac{8}{12}, \dots$ — by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by any non-zero integer. There are infinitely many such integers to multiply by, so there are infinitely many forms too. But when we say that the denominator must be positive AND the HCF must be 1, only one pair is left each time — in this case, (2, 3). That is why the standard form is unique and is a reliable way to compare two numbers.
